newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Rubin warns China of difficulties over MFN renewal.
newsitem.headline: Rubin warns China of difficulties over MFN renewal.

text.p: U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin, stressing the importance of human rights in China and the maintenance of broad freedoms in Hong Kong, warned Beijing on Sunday that the Clinton administration faced a tough time in winning renewal of its trade privileges.

"This is going to be a more difficult process this time than last," Rubin said he told Chinese Finance Minister Liu Zhongli during an hour-long meeting on the fringes of a gathering of Asia-Pacific finance ministers.
The Clinton administration has already made clear that it will seek Congressional approval of most favoured nation (MFN) trading privilieges for China when they come up for annual renewal in June.

But allegations that China illegally tried to influence the 1996 presidential election, coupled with ongoing concerns about its human rights record and large trade surplus with the United States, mean Congressional approval is not assured.

Rubin said he did not raise the allegations of illegal campaign contributions in his meeting with Liu, noting that the issue had already been aired with the Chinese by Vice President Al Gore and Secretary of State Madeleine Albright.

He said that about half of his meeting, which had originally been scheduled for half an hour, was taken up by a discussion of human rights in China and by Hong Kong, which will be handed over to Beijing by Britain on July 1.

Rubin, a former Wall Street executive, argued that international banks and other financial institutions would take account of the rule of law, freeom of expression and human rights in Hong Kong in deciding how much of a presence to have there after the handover.
Liu listened intently to Rubin's comments, but made no clear response, according to the U.S. Treasury chief.

Rubin said he also highlighted the importance that the United States attaches to human rights issues and told the Chinese finance minister that they would play a major role in the Congressional debate on MFN.
"There will be a heightened focus on that in the context of the MFN debate," Rubin said.
China's bulging trade surplus with the United States, which rose 17 percent last year to $40 billion, is also expected to feature prominently in that debate.
"The trade imbalance between our two countries is an issue of great importance," Rubin said. "There clearly are trade impediments that need to be addressed."
He told Liu he also wants to investigate the impact that each country's broad economic policies may have had on the bilateral trade imbalance.
China, seeking to avoid an overheating of its economy, slowed growth to a roughly nine percent last year, and that may have dampened its demand for imports.
Rubin said he did not discuss with Liu China's bid to join the World Trade Organisation. The United States has said it supports Chinese membership in the trade body, but on commercial grounds.

The Treasury chief though made clear that China needed to promise to open up and liberalise its financial markets as the price of entry to the WTO. But U.S. officials have noted in the past that that process could be phased in over a number of years.
Rubin and Liu though did agree to hold a meeting of the two countries' Joint Economic Committee in Beijing in the fall, possibly in late September.
The meeting would take place ahead of a planned November summit between U.S. President Bill Clinton and Chinese President Jiang Zemin.
The committee, which discusses a broad range of economic issues, last met in November, in Washington.
